subject: chemistry_2
question_text: How does PCl₃ react with a) CH₃COOH b) C₂H₅OH and c) water

verification.note: Unit 7 (VA Group Elements) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.83-84, from the shaded sub-box "VA GROUP ELEMENTS" of printed chapter 7 ("7. VA, VIA, VIIA GROUP ELEMENTS & NOBLE GASES"); the book prints this question and all three equations on book p.83 as VSAQ 15. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK CHECK (book p.83, VSAQ 15): all three printed equations were atom-counted and all three are balanced. PCl₃ + 3CH₃COOH → 3CH₃COCl + H₃PO₃ (P 1, Cl 3, C 6, H 12, O 6 each side); PCl₃ + 3C₂H₅OH → 3C₂H₅Cl + H₃PO₃ (P 1, Cl 3, C 6, H 18, O 3 each side); PCl₃ + 3H₂O → H₃PO₃ + 3HCl (P 1, Cl 3, H 6, O 3 each side). They are reproduced unchanged. BOOK GAP: the book prints the three equations with no sentence at all, so nothing tells the reader that the same thing happens in all three — PCl₃ replaces an –OH group by –Cl, and the phosphorus always ends as H₃PO₃. That unifying line is added. The book also prints the chlorine in "PCl₃" in a mixed italic on this page, which is a typesetting artefact and not a chemical distinction.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: With acetic acid and ethanol
lines: a) With acetic acid it gives acetyl chloride:
b) With ethanol it gives ethyl chloride:
steps.why: One idea covers both parts: any compound with an –OH group has that group replaced by –Cl, and the three chlorine atoms of PCl₃ do it three times over. That is why the coefficient is 3 in both equations and why the phosphorus product is the same in both.
common_mistakes: Writing CH₃COCl as CH₃COOCl. Acetyl chloride has one oxygen; the –OH has been replaced by –Cl.
Using a coefficient of 1 instead of 3. PCl₃ has three chlorine atoms, so it converts three –OH groups.
steps.memory_tip: One –OH out, one –Cl in, three times over. The phosphorus is left as H₃PO₃ every time.
steps.margin_note: Both equations belong in this step. Balanced coefficients of 3 are what the mark checks.

steps.label: With water
lines: c) Water also has an –OH group, so PCl₃ is
The products are phosphorous acid and
hydrogen chloride, which fumes in moist air.
steps.why: Water is the simplest compound with an –OH group, so it follows the same pattern as the acid and the alcohol and gives H₃PO₃ once more. Note the contrast with PCl₅, which with a little cold water gives POCl₃ and only with excess water gives H₃PO₄.
common_mistakes: Giving H₃PO₄ as the product. PCl₃ gives phosphorous acid H₃PO₃; H₃PO₄ comes from PCl₅.
Writing 3H₂O as H₂O. Three water molecules are needed for three chlorine atoms.
steps.memory_tip: PCl₃ with water gives H₃PO₃; PCl₅ with excess water gives H₃PO₄. Count the O atoms.
steps.margin_note: This equation alone earns the mark. Write the names of the two products if there is room.

insider_note: All three parts are one reaction: PCl₃ replaces –OH by –Cl and is itself left as H₃PO₃. Write that sentence once at the top and the three equations follow from it.
